title: A Food Trip Around Lithuania
summary: You travel to four famous places in Lithuania, try one special dish in each, and learn why each place and each dish is famous.

blocks.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Today you take a trip around Lithuania. You visit four famous places and try one special dish in each. You also learn how to order food, buy tickets and ask questions.

blocks.title: Warm-up

items.prompt: Which famous places in your country do visitors love?
Which dish from your country do you want a visitor to try?
Do you like to eat new food when you travel?

blocks.title: Part 1: Vilnius Old Town and Cepelinai
paragraphs: Your trip starts in Vilnius, the capital of Lithuania. You walk through the Old Town. The streets are small, and there are old churches everywhere. This Old Town is very old, and it is also very big. Many of its buildings and streets are hundreds of years old. Because of this, UNESCO put it on its World Heritage list. UNESCO is a world group that takes care of very important places.

At lunch, you go into Etno Dvaras, a restaurant with food from Lithuania. You order cepelinai, the national dish of Lithuania. Cepelinai are big potato dumplings. A dumpling is a soft ball of food with more food inside. Inside cepelinai, there is usually meat or curd cheese, a soft white cheese. On top, there is a sauce of sour cream with small pieces of bacon.

Why the funny name? A zeppelin is a long, round flying ship. It carries people, like a plane. Cepelinai have the same long, round shape. So people named them after the zeppelin. At Etno Dvaras, one plate of cepelinai costs 9.55 euros.

images.alt: A white plate with two long, round potato dumplings covered in sour cream sauce and small bacon pieces, on a table by a window to an old stone street with churches

blocks.title: Check: Part 1: Vilnius Old Town and Cepelinai

items.prompt: Why do people call this dish cepelinai?
items.answer: It looks like a zeppelin: long and round.

blocks.title: Useful phrases

rows.example: Hello! Can I see the menu?
These look good. What is inside?

blocks.title: Part 2: Trakai Island Castle and Kibinai
paragraphs: The next day, you take a train from Vilnius to Trakai. Trakai Island Castle stands on a small island in a lake. You walk to it over a bridge. The castle is red and more than 600 years old. Inside, there is a museum about the history of Lithuania.

After the castle, you go to Karaimų Street to try kibinai. Kibinai are small pastries. Inside, there is meat and onion. The traditional meat is mutton, the meat of an adult sheep. Kibinai are the food of the Karaim people. In English, Karaimų Street is Street of the Karaim.

Who are the Karaim? More than 600 years ago, Vytautas was the ruler of Lithuania. He brought Karaim families to Trakai from Crimea, a place far in the south. Their job was to keep his castle safe. Vytautas gave them land here, and they lived on this street. That is why the street has their name. They brought their own food with them, and kibinai were part of it. A small group of Karaim people still lives in Trakai today.

images.alt: Golden half-moon pastries filled with meat on a wooden board, with a red brick castle on a lake behind

rows.example: Hello! How much is it for a student?

Excuse me! Where can I buy kibinai?

blocks.title: Part 3: The Hill of Crosses and Šaltibarščiai
paragraphs: On day three, you go north to the city of Šiauliai. The Hill of Crosses is a short drive from the city. From far away, it looks like a small hill. Up close, you see crosses everywhere, big and small, wooden and metal. Today, there are more than 100,000 crosses on the hill.

Why are they here? In the 1800s, many people in Lithuania died in fights against Russia. They wanted their country to be free. Their families never found the bodies. So the families had no place to visit and remember them. Instead, they put crosses on this hill.

Later, Lithuania was part of the Soviet Union. The Soviet leaders did not want people to pray. So they did not want the crosses. Again and again, they destroyed the crosses on the hill. The first time, in 1961, they destroyed all the crosses in one day. Crosses on the hill were against the law, and people were punished for them. But people came back at night and put up new crosses. In the dark, it was harder to see them, but it was still dangerous. They came anyway. So the hill became a sign that the people did not give up.

After your visit, you eat lunch in Šiauliai. It is a hot July day, so you order šaltibarščiai. This is a famous cold pink soup. It is made with beetroot and kefir. Beetroot is a dark red vegetable, and it makes the soup pink. Kefir is a thick milk drink, a little like yogurt. People eat this soup on hot summer days, with boiled potatoes on the side.

images.alt: A small hill covered with thousands of wooden and metal crosses of many sizes and hanging rosaries, under a cloudy sky

blocks.title: Part 4: The Curonian Spit and Smoked Fish
paragraphs: Your last stop is the Curonian Spit. A spit is a long, thin piece of land in the sea. On one side is the Baltic Sea. On the other is the Curonian Lagoon. A lagoon is a big, quiet area of water next to the sea. There is land in between. To get there, you take a short ferry from the city of Klaipėda. It goes to Smiltynė, at the north end of the spit. Then you take a bus to Nida. The ride is about one hour. In the village of Nida, you climb the Parnidis Dune. A dune is a hill of sand that the wind makes. It is 52 metres high. From the top, you see sand, forest and water on both sides.

In the 1800s, fishing was the most important work in Nida. People caught fish in the lagoon. But there were no fridges then, and fish goes bad fast. So they smoked the fish over a fire. Smoke dries the fish, so it stays OK to eat for longer. They often used the wood of the alder tree. Its smoke is soft and sweet, and it makes the fish golden. Today, small shops all over the spit sell smoked fish.

In Nida, you go to a café called Tik pas Joną. In English, the name is Only at Jonas's Place. This café smokes its own fish. You choose bream, a fish from the lagoon, or eel. An eel is a long fish that looks like a snake. The fish is still warm, and you eat it with bread and your hands.

images.alt: One whole golden smoked bream (a deep, flat-sided lagoon fish with a tall body) next to a golden smoked eel (long and thin like a snake), on brown paper on a wooden table outdoors, with slices of dark rye bread, and a tall pale sand dune and calm lagoon water behind

blocks.title: Scene: Lunch at Etno Dvaras
paragraphs: You walk around the Old Town all morning. Now you are hungry. You sit down at Etno Dvaras, and a waiter comes to your table.
Your goal: order cepelinai, ask what is inside, and pay the bill.

blocks.title: Conversation: Lunch at Etno Dvaras

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Hello! Can I see the menu, please?

turns.speaker: Waiter
turns.text: Of course. Here you are.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Thank you. I would like cepelinai, please.

turns.speaker: Waiter
turns.text: Great choice. They are our most famous dish.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: What is inside?

turns.speaker: Waiter
turns.text: Meat or curd cheese. Which one do you want?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Meat, please. How much is it?

turns.speaker: Waiter
turns.text: 9.55 euros. It comes with sour cream on top.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Great, thank you.

turns.speaker: Waiter
turns.text: Here are your cepelinai. Enjoy!

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: That was delicious. The bill, please.

turns.speaker: Waiter
turns.text: Here you are. That is 9.55 euros.

blocks.title: Scene: A Ticket for Trakai Castle
paragraphs: It is a sunny afternoon in July. You walk over the bridge to Trakai Island Castle. Ona sells tickets at the ticket office.
Your goal: buy a ticket. Then ask when the castle closes and where to eat kibinai.

blocks.title: Conversation: A Ticket for Trakai Castle

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Hello. One adult ticket, please.

turns.speaker: Ona
turns.text: Hello! That is 14 euros.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: How much is it for a student?

turns.speaker: Ona
turns.text: Students pay 7 euros.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: OK, one adult ticket. Here you are. What time do you close?

turns.speaker: Ona
turns.text: In July, we close at 7 p.m.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Great. Where can I buy kibinai after my visit?

turns.speaker: Ona
turns.text: Go to Kybynlar. It is at number 29 on Karaimų Street.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Thank you very much!

blocks.title: Scene: Asking a Local at the Hill of Crosses
paragraphs: You walk between thousands of crosses. Rūta, a woman from Šiauliai, is putting a small cross on the hill.
Your goal: ask about the crosses, and ask if you can add one.

blocks.title: Conversation: Asking a Local at the Hill of Crosses

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Hi! Excuse me. Can I ask you something?

turns.speaker: Rūta
turns.text: Yes, of course.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: How many crosses are there?

turns.speaker: Rūta
turns.text: Nobody can count them all. There are more than 100,000.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Why do people bring crosses here?

turns.speaker: Rūta
turns.text: To remember someone, or to pray.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Is it OK to put up my own cross?

turns.speaker: Rūta
turns.text: Yes. A wooden cross up to 2 metres tall is fine.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Do I need to ask anyone first?

turns.speaker: Rūta
turns.text: Not for a small cross. For a taller one, you ask first.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Thank you so much!

blocks.title: Scene: Smoked Fish in Nida
paragraphs: After the dune, you walk to Tik pas Joną. It is midday, and the fish is still warm. You meet the cook.
Your goal: choose a fish. Then ask where it is from and how to eat it.

blocks.title: Conversation: Smoked Fish in Nida

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Hello! What is good here today?

turns.speaker: Cook
turns.text: Today we have bream and eel. Try the bream first.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: OK. Is it from here?

turns.speaker: Cook
turns.text: Yes. It is from the Curonian Lagoon, right next to Nida.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Do you smoke it here?

turns.speaker: Cook
turns.text: Yes, we smoke all our own fish here.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: How do you eat it?

turns.speaker: Cook
turns.text: With bread, and with your hands. No fork.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Mmm! It is delicious!

turns.speaker: Cook
turns.text: Thank you! At midday, the fish is still warm.

blocks.title: Speaking
paragraphs: Work with a partner. Student A is back from a trip to Lithuania. Student B is a friend and asks questions. Student A tells the story of the trip in order, from Vilnius to Nida. For each place, Student A talks about one dish and one fact. Student B asks two questions about each place, like How much was the ticket? Then change roles. After that, act out one scene together, like buying the castle ticket.

blocks.title: Final Reflection
blocks.intro: You saw four places in four days, and every dish had a story.

items.prompt: Which place do you want to visit first, and why?
Which dish do you want to try most?
Which place or dish reminds you of something in Japan?
